video_title: Scaling Laws: Meta's Big Investment in Workforce Training
transcript: Rosemary, welcome to Scaling Laws. >> Thank you for having me, Kevin. I'm excited to be here. >> So, we're talking a few days after the election here in DC. And usually when you think about DC, you think about how does a bill become a law. But I want to talk about how an AI model gets deployed and in particular how we build the AI tech stack because often times when people think about AI, they think, oh, you know, uh, agents and they think about frontier AI and they think about swarms now. But there's a lot of infrastructure that goes into AI. So you head up the workforce and infrastructure initiative here at Meta. Can you tell us just a little bit more for the folks who don't pay attention to the AI tech stack? What's at the very bottom? What are the the pipes, the wires, the buildings? What do we need to actually have AI? >> Yeah, that's a great question. I think a lot of people think about AI and the workforce that's needed to build this out as super tech-savvy folks. Um, and we do need that, of course. Um, >> we always need nerds. >> We always need nerds. But we also need a lot of people who um who build this stuff um who are going to build out the AI infrastructure across the United States. If we want to remain globally competitive, especially in the race to AI, the US has got to have some of the top uh infrastructure that's required. And that really means people who are using their hands um the skilled trades. And I think for the first time over the past decade or so, Meta has really started to get its feet wet in this whole construction and skilled trades world that I'm not sure it ever knew it would be such a big player in. Um which is really exciting. Um but the fact is is we just don't have enough workers to do this kind of work. Um so we've been looking at things like fiber technician training and construction training. Um getting people really at the ground level to to help to help with this out. Yeah, I rewatched the social network in preparation for this interview and I don't recall Mark at all mentioning that, you know, one day we're going to lead a workforce academy for construction jobs and yet here we are. And to your point in terms of the skills shortage, I think it's really important to put this in perspective of the fact that we know from the Association of Builders and Contractors that there's hundreds of thousands of net jobs in construction that are expected in the coming years. And we also know from the Bureau of Labor and Statistics that we need 72,000 electricians. And so maybe a question that comes to mind immediately for why is Meta working on this issue. Why wasn't that skills gap being met previously? >> Yeah, I think um there's a number of reasons as to how we've ended up in a massive shortage um in this country and we can kind of go into some of those, but >> we'll get into the weeds. >> Okay. But I think the the truth is is it takes a long time to become a skilled electrician. Um and we want that. We want experts who know how to wire a home. We don't want people to to end up in a situation where a fire breaks out or something along those lines. Um and but to get there, we've got to we've got to start to really open the pathway for a lot more people to enter into that. Um we've really sort of kept a a close um a tight funnel on some of this stuff. Um, so I think for Meta, we definitely need more journeymen and electricians. We need high uh highly skilled HVAC operators and pipe fitters, um, plumbers. But the truth is is we can't do that overnight. You can't just train that overnight. And so what we're really trying to do is open up the talent pool at the entry level, the frontline workforce, um to get more people into that so that we then get them on to the registered apprenticeships, the craft journeyman trade career tracks, um so that we get more uh electricians and the like um over time. So you just mentioned so many different jobs and so many new professions. Well, not new professions, but new applications of these professions in the AI space to meet this surge in demand for that infrastructure for getting into the weeds. What is America's Workforce Academy? Because folks may have seen an ad about this launching in Ohio, Indiana, Louisiana, and Texas. Maybe somebody knows somebody who's even joined the program. But for the listeners who are just hearing about do we shorthand it as the AWA is is that okay? All right. We'll call it the AWA. What is it? What does it entail? Just from a nuts andbolts perspective. >> It is one of the most unique employer-driven job training programs I've ever sort of seen. And I've been in workforce development uh for most of my career. So I it at its basic level it is a 4-week training program um designed to help people quickly enter the skilled trades. Meta had decided had determined um years ago we we started with fiber technicians. We desperately needed fiber technicians and we've been funding tons of education and training programs across the country to do that and we continue to do that by the way with community colleges with universities with other training providers but it's just not moving fast enough. And so we decided at a certain point we were going to bring some of this stuff inhouse. And so we created a four-week training program alongside CBRE um to uh uh bring people who had very few uh um technical skills um into this field. And it's built on two big premises. A we will guarantee you a job on the front end um which is sort of unheard of and as long as you pass uh the training or complete the training. And then the second thing is is we will pay you a wage while you're in the training. And those two key components, I think, are leading to results that we never would have even imagined. We've got over 90% completion rates in the four weeks of training. A good workforce development program, Kevin, is usually around 65 75% completion rate. Those are some of our stellar ones in the country. This is over 90%. And I think it's really because of those two issues. And then the second thing is I've got now at to date I've got 500 people um across the country on AI infrastructure sites working um who are making significantly more than they were when they entered the program and are now on career pathways like we talked about to becoming uh full-time journeymen um etc uh where they can really have quite a lucrative career. >> So let's get even further into the weeds as promised. Let's say I decide that, you know, this whole professor gig, it's not for me anymore. And I I gave it my best shot, but the student evals, they just said my jokes were too bad. And so the dean cuts me loose. And I'm thinking, huh, well, here's a growing industry. I saw the AWA is in Houston, Texas. I'll just drive over to Houston and start this program. Do I have to have prior experience in doing fiber work or get my hands dirty in construction? What are the eligibility standards for people who want to get involved? >> It's actually very little. Um, we are really pulling people um from all walks of life. So, we are finding people who are mid-career changers, people who are in their 40s and 50s who just sort of say, you know what, I really want to do something different or I'm worried that maybe the industry I've been in may be changing so rapidly and and this is one I know that is very stable. Um, we've also got people who are right out of high school who um don't, you know, are looking for a career that maybe they hadn't even thought that they could access before. Um, so we've got all kinds of folks that are entering, veterans, um, uh, uh, a whole host of folks. We've got the the eligibility requirements are are very few. You do not have to have any experience in the skilled trades. You, uh, have to have a high school diploma for the most most cases. Um, but not always, quite frankly. And then we go through the the intake and the recruitment process. We're working with our contractor partners and they have their own hiring requirements. Um but to be quite frank, um we're we're finding people with all kinds of skill levels who are injured. >> Okay. So even someone as unskilled as myself, as my wife can attest to, I'm like, how quickly can I get on Task Rabbit to find someone to fix this dishwasher? But that's a that's another conversation. Uh so even someone like me can join and then I enter into a 4-week program. So, this isn't meant to say, "Hey, over four weeks all of the sudden I am the world's best electrician." Tell me more about what this is supposed to actually prepare folks for. What does it set them up for? What does it result in in terms of a credential or anything like that? >> That's exactly right. We are not pretending that we are creating full-term full journeymen electricians in four weeks. Um, but what we are doing is we are getting you the skills and the credentials necessary to get into the workforce. um you have the proper safety certifications. We're working with NCCER, the national uh rec uh validator of uh in the construction industry around um around their certifications. We get you OSHA 10, those types of certifications that get you into the work work site. Once you're on the work site, then of course there's uh on the job training that happens with the contractors. There's uh apprenticeship tracks that you can get put onto. So that the training never actually ends. But the four weeks we are doing is getting people who have very little to no experience in the construction trade into it. Um and that's been I think one of the biggest barriers um to growing the trades and to helping to fill the shortage is because a lot of people just don't even know how to access it or can't they can't afford it and they don't have the time to take um we're providing access to that. >> And so not only are you guaranteeing a job which I want to talk about more in a second but I've I've managed to get into the pro program you all accepted this lowly professor. Uh, I'm studying to go into the fiber world. Uh, over this 4-week period, am I covering my own cost? Where am I staying? Who's covering that? Are my meals covered? What's that all look like? >> The whole thing is taken care of. Um, from the beginning of the recruitment process, if we bring you in, uh, if we bring you, if you've been enrolled, um, we will pay for your travel to the training. We will pay for your lodging during the training during the four weeks. We will pay you meals, a a stipen. Um we will also pay you a wage and that wage is around $25 an hour um for an individual uh to be to be in this program. And then of course on the front end you are guaranteed a job. So by the day you graduate that Friday, that very next Monday, you are likely on site at a new at a a job working full-time. Um so those are Yeah. I mean, from I don't soup, nuts to bolts, >> nuts to soup, bolts, nuts. I don't know. I've never understood. Who wants bolts in their soup or vice versa? Never understood it either. >> It's not going to work well. But speaking of work, to get back on track, uh, what's the catch? This sounds too good. You know, oh, four weeks paid for meals, 90% completion rate. Uh, why are you investing 115 million just for this first year? And and we can talk about your future plans. Why does it make sense for Meta to be investing that much in a program that again almost sounds too good to be true to be blunt? >> Yeah. I I mean I don't think there's any secret about it. We were desperate for workers. Like it's just that's basically what it came down to. We needed really highly qualified people. We weren't moving fast enough and some of the avenues we were pursuing. So we decided to also do this. It's another pathway I think into getting into the skilled trades because we are so desperate for it. The other thing too, Kevin, is is we're making massive investments across this across this country when it comes to the AI infrastructure buildout. And part of that massive investment is investing in people. Um, it's probably the biggest investment we're going to make. And I think Meta fully recognizes that. And so as we're thinking about the way the places we're going to and the places we're going to build out, we are thinking about the people who live in those places, ensuring they are prioritized to work at these sites. These are long-term projects. In fact, when we start in a in a community, um it's not just the the initial buildout. We do expansions over time. There's maintenance. Um these are long-term jobs, and so we want to make sure that the people who live there have the skills to work there. Um and that's a commitment that Meta uh has made a promise to and is fulfilling. Let's talk more about the jobs that folks are walking into and how that overlaps with demands that we're seeing from unions in terms of the needs they have for their workforces and the needs of uh the folks who are building data centers who are creating that infrastructure. What's that look like and how are you partnering with those entities? So, Meta uh operates a number of sites across the country and we work with both union and non-union contractors and so the training we are doing make sure that we fulfill both of those contractors um missions. Um many of the students who are going through the program um they they will get offers from both union and non-UN shops. And so with the union shops in particular, we will often have at the hiring event, the local affiliate, the local union affiliate like the local IBEW, the electricians union will be alongside the contractor offering employment and offering um uh entry into the union um on the same day. So we're seeing sort of both of this happening at the same time. We've got associated builders and contractors who are doing a lot of the training, but we're also partnering with a lot of union shops um and local union affiliates to do the work. So, putting on my public policy 101 hat, I believe the term would be crowding out. Is there a concern that Meta's involvement here, saying we're going to be the ones who step into the shoes of what people may say, hey, that's the role of community colleges or hey, that's the role of trade schools or fill in the blank a public entity doing this work. What's the case, the public policy case for why Meta has to intercede here or why we need a private part of this broader workforce solution to America's skills shortage? >> I think there's always uh there's multiple ways in which people can access and get highquality training. This is one path. It's not the only path. I certainly think META will be working does work with community colleges all across this country. We'll continue to do that. My hope is is that we will scale this and build this out with more traditional education partners over time for sustainability. But the truth is is that um we needed we need to move fast and our education system sometimes uh doesn't move at the speed of business. >> What? >> No, I know. >> Oh my gosh, you heard it here first, folks. >> Um so I think as as they start as the world is sort of changing so rapidly due to technology, they too are starting to change their models. this is a model we would like for them to look at and partner with us on. Um and I have every belief that that is where we will get the most innovative uh educational institutions in this country do get that and we are working with them. Um and my hope is that over time we'll see we'll see it start to scale. >> I want to go back to something you said earlier which was for traditional workforce development programs the completion rate was a D. 67% of folks getting through those programs. And you and I have chatted previously, this is not your first rodeo in workforce development. And you mentioned a phrase that's kept me up at night uh at times, which was train and pray. The idea that, hey, we're going to provide this training, we're going to help upskill this person, and then we're going to pray that it all works out, which doesn't sound like good public policy or what's in the interest of anyone. uh both the folks looking for jobs and the folks looking to hire. So walk me a little bit more through the history of America's to be blunt failures on workforce development and why we even have a phrase like train and prey. >> Oftentimes I think it comes down to one key component which is the employer is often left uh out of the entire design and development of all of this. Um, and so what happens is we build these programs. Many of them are probably well-intentioned and are probably pretty decent. Um, but there's no actual link to demand on the other end. Um, and so that's why I think we have so many people going into job training programs with no um, no guarantee on the other end that it will actually lead to something that could lead to a self a family sustaining career, which is why most people enter. um we develop a lot of training programs I think with good intentions but at the end of the day they don't um they don't actually meet why the person entered into the first place. It's why I was excited to come to Meta in the first to come to Meta generally because it was really sort of saying we're not just going to invest in workforce development. We're not just going to invest in the skilled trades. There's a lot of folks that are putting money into the skilled trades and that's wonderful and that's good. But we're actually going to impact people directly and we are going to say if you do if you complete this job that actually has the skills that lead to work at a meta site, you will have a job and you could have a job for the rest of your life. Um, and that's uh it's sort of unheard of in this world. And I think that the key component has always been the guaranteed job on the front end and that the training matches what the job description requires. And this is where for listeners who are loving that we're nerding into this conversation to nerd out further about those failures. We've seen historically that the incentives just don't necessarily align between the entity that's doing the workforce training and the individual going through it. Often times, for example, they there's a specification that the trainer helped the individual find the first available job. And we're kind of measuring, hey, how quickly can you find work? Well, that might not be the job that the person was actually looking for. It may not be sustainable. It may not be renumerative. And so, changing those incentives and expanding our imagination to say something like, hey, we see the need for jobs in the sector, we're going to guarantee you a job. Not only is then assurance for the employers who now have a better sense of are we going to be able to meet our skills demands but then if I'm thinking of Americans who many of whom feel a lot of economic uncertainty right now and the idea that I would say hey you know I've been a law professor for however long and now I'm just going to jump ship and go into this new burgeoning industry. If you don't have those asurances, to your point earlier, that's a that's a really big risk for your family, for your community. And so, as we more generally think about how to restructure workforce training, this seems like a really promising model, and I'm I'm eager to hear from you, you all have been at this for a year. This was the the first pilot. Are are people coming out of the woodwork saying, "Hey, Rosemary, what are you up to? How can we emulate this? How can we get involved?" Yeah, we've only been at it for six months. >> Okay. All right. All right. I'm sorry. Yeah, >> we move at the speed of light here at Meta. So, >> there we go. As you should. >> As you should. Um, which is exciting because it means we can we can pivot pretty quickly. If things aren't working, we can sort of make changes. Um, I we are seeing people sort of come out of the woodwork. Um, the one thing I would just sort of go back and say is a lot of people thought, oh, are these are these good jobs? People don't really want to do this kind of work. When we launched in July, we had about a thousand fiber tech jobs that we were trying to fill with the training. We had 35,000 people apply within the first week. I mean, it was pretty wild. Today, we have over 100,000 people that have applied for both the fiber tech training and what we're calling our construction ready training, which is like a construction generalist. Um, so we know that the demand for these jobs is out there. People really want to do it. It's just there's a lot of barriers, I think, into getting into this field. to your point on workforce development, especially at the federal level, and how how we've thought about it as a nation for a long time, is rightfully or wrongfully, most of our programs funnel people into two and four-year degree programs. And we have the best universities in the world. I want to continue to have the best universities in the world. They lead to good jobs, but it's not a pathway for everybody. And we know that we've seen a lot of people go down that pathway who don't complete, who are left with a lot of debt and who don't have any skills or credentials to show for it. Um, so we've got to rethink I think some of these models and we've got to make sure that we're talking to people about where they are and what they actually want, which is a family sustaining career in most cases. And so how do you get them on that path and how do you do it quickly? Um, and so uh, yeah, I think we're just we're it's one model. Um, I think we're we're open to always continuing to think and pivot and and restructure as necessary. We want to work with more partners. My goal is to work with a lot of other corporations who want the same kind of workforce um so that we're all rowing in the same direction and helping more and more people out because we know the demand is is there. >> So, you mentioned you have uh the association of builders and contractors focused on that construction readiness pipeline. Then we have CBRE working on fiber. Uh you mentioned earlier though we need more pipe fitters, we need more plumbers, we need more electricians. Is the plan to expand to those domains or are you is this a 1-800 please call META to get involved? Are you actively recruiting additional partners to help expand this program? >> We're always looking for additional partners. I would say we know um these contractors especially with the unions uh the big unions IBW NAB 2 they've got some of the gold standard in training already. I don't know if I need to go and recreate how to become an a registered election electric electrical apprentice. Um my goal is to try and funnel more people into those programs um so that we can then hire them. Um and that that is what we're doing. So we're looking at obviously uh funding many of that many of those programs and we do already Kevin um in a lot of cases. My goal right now is to just open up the aperture for people who never would have accessed to get them into the pipeline initially. So undoubtedly at some point in time you've received some push back of you know it's Meta I have some concerns because of XY andZ policy reason or XY andZ prior event. I'm a little uh unsure of whether we should partner with with Meta. What are some of the push back you've received and how have you countered those narratives? Yeah, I mean you know meta is at the forefront of uh of the sort of technological revolution that's happening in this country. Um we have I think uh a front row seat to how how the work and the workforce is going to change. Um there's always push back I think and there's and some of it's you know surely right rightfully so. I think we can be good community partners and we want to be good community partners um to make sure that this country remains um at the forefront of all of this. Meta is committed to doing that. And so uh what I have found every day is that people actually want want to be partners. They want this stuff to work. they want uh they want the AI infrastructure out there so that they have we have medical breakthroughs and we um you know uh solve for problems that we've been trying to solve for for years. Um at the same time we're trying to ensure that people who um uh um people who who don't know how to get into into some of this have their first step in into building some of this stuff out. And so that's been one of our biggest um goals. >> Yeah. So, we've been talking for a minute and I haven't mentioned the dword, which is data centers. Uh you know, it's it's become a bit of a four-letter word for a lot of Americans. And we saw just a little over a week ago a lot of Americans vote in a way that would either place a moratorum on data centers or otherwise impose barriers on their development. So we're seeing the benefit, the economic benefits of what happens in a community when we're working together alongside them. In terms of the workforce, I have gone to Richland Parish now to recruit individuals from that area, that whole region to work at that center. Um, and we had over 200 people come out in August, uh, wanting these jobs, right? So that I don't I don't doubt for a second. >> Yeah. Uh like you said, for a small rural community to be a hub now for talented individuals, that's a great story to tell, but it often doesn't break through. Things that never would have happened before.
